strengths: The paper presents a simple, interpretable idea: train a normalized linear probe in a shared foundation-model embedding space and map its class directions back to human-readable concepts.
The proposed pipeline is lightweight and clearly structured, and the experiments span four datasets across both image and text modalities.
Reporting both worst-group and average accuracy is useful, and the paper includes limited ablations of the scoring rule and number of retained concepts.
The appendix states relevant limitations of captioning and keyword extraction and appropriately recommends human oversight for consequential uses.
weaknesses: The central framing around weight-update trajectories is not substantiated: the proposed score uses only the final probe weights, does not analyze the trajectory, and does not establish that class-text initialization is necessary. Moreover, the method analyzes a newly trained linear probe rather than the internal decision process of a generally fine-tuned foundation model.

Equation 3 uses the minimum similarity among competing classes. In a multiclass problem, discrimination against the strongest competitor requires a maximum; the proposed minimum can give a high score to a concept that is equally predictive of another class merely because it is dissimilar to an unrelated class. The generic cosine bound in Equation 2 does not establish concept presence, causal influence, or spuriousness.

The evaluation does not directly measure bias discovery. There is no precision, recall, ranking metric, expert assessment, or counterfactual intervention against known spurious attributes. Several reported concepts are legitimate class attributes, generic words, or questionable outputs, and the paper itself says the newly discovered biases only “might” be correct.

Improved zero-shot prompting is an indirect and confounded proxy for bias quality: taking a maximum over many class-specific prompts can help recognition even when concepts are not biases. Random concepts, frequency-based concepts, class-similarity rankings, oracle prompts, and matched prompt-ensemble controls are absent.

Comparisons are incomplete: most competing methods are evaluated on only one or two datasets, with no baseline results on NICO++ or CivilComments. There are also no multiple-run statistics, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite claims of significant and state-of-the-art improvements.

The claimed accuracy improvement obscures substantial tradeoffs. Average accuracy decreases from 90.7 to 84.7 on Waterbirds, 88.4 to 86.2 on NICO++, and 83.4 to 69.0 on CivilComments; only worst-group accuracy consistently rises, and the resulting fairness–accuracy tradeoff is not analyzed.

Reproducibility is insufficient: the paper does not fully specify splits and group definitions for several datasets, training duration and seeds, CivilComments decision thresholds, how the cutoff of 15 was selected, or whether concept extraction uses training data or the “full dataset” stated in Table 4. No code or complete per-dataset baseline protocol is provided.

strengths: The core idea is simple, interpretable, and computationally practical: train a normalized linear probe initialized from class-name embeddings, then rank textual concepts against its learned weights.

The paper addresses an important problem and evaluates both vision and language settings across Waterbirds, CelebA, NICO++, and CivilComments. The reported worst-group gains over basic zero-shot prompting are substantial on several datasets.
The presentation is generally clear, with a useful overview figure, an explicit scoring rule, implementation hyperparameters, prompt templates, qualitative outputs, and limited ablations.
The authors acknowledge important dependencies on caption quality, keyword extraction, concept hierarchies, and human review.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is not established. Even for an unbiased dataset, the optimal linear-classifier weight need not equal the class-name embedding because of modality gaps, label wording, and legitimate intra-class variation. Moreover, the proposed score uses only final weights—not the drift trajectory or even the initialization—so the experiments do not show that drift specifically identifies bias. Random-initialization, class-initialization, trajectory, and no-training controls are missing.

Equation 2 is a generic and potentially loose geometric bound; it does not establish that a concept causally influences predictions. In multiclass settings, subtracting the minimum similarity to another class rewards separation from the least similar competitor, whereas discrimination normally depends on the most competitive alternative. This can assign high scores to concepts shared by several classes.

The main evaluation is indirect: extracted concepts are assessed by modifying zero-shot prompts for the foundational model rather than by verifying their influence on the trained probe whose weights supposedly contain the biases. There are no interventions, counterfactual tests, concept-removal experiments, annotations, or precision/recall measurements against known spurious attributes.

The prompt evaluation is under-specified and potentially confounded. Taking a maximum over templates favors methods producing more candidates, prompt budgets are not matched, and the choice of 15 concepts appears benchmark-sensitive without a held-out selection protocol. It is also unclear whether concept extraction ever accesses test data.

Comparisons are incomplete: most competing methods are reported on only one or two datasets, with no competing bias-discovery results for NICO++ or CivilComments. Essential baselines such as ranking concepts using class embeddings, class centroids, a conventionally initialized probe, or direct concept-frequency statistics are absent, so the claimed state-of-the-art advantage is not demonstrated.

The paper reports no seeds, uncertainty, or significance tests despite claiming significant improvements. Group construction and evaluation details are insufficient, especially for CivilComments, and several training and extraction details needed for reproduction are missing.

Average accuracy decreases on three of four datasets, dramatically on CivilComments from 83.4% to 69.0%, but the fairness–utility tradeoff is not analyzed. Thus the claim of broadly improved zero-shot performance is overstated.

Many qualitative outputs are generic, label-related, or ambiguous rather than validated biases. Treating identity and religion terms in CivilComments as discovered biases without subgroup or human evaluation also risks reinforcing harmful associations. Generalization to “any other modality” is unsupported by experiments limited to image and text data.
